ai-at-work.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
ai-at-work.excerpt: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Signal is now blocking screenshot functionality on its mobile apps to prevent users from capturing messages that could be used to train AI surveillance systems. This matters to digital workplace pros because it highlights an emerging security concern: even encrypted communications can be compromised if employees screenshot sensitive conversations and those images end up in datasets. Honestly, this feels like plugging a leak in the Titanic. If your organization relies on Signal for confidential discussions, you've got bigger problems than whether someone can screencap it.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: TechCrunch rounded up AI agents that operate through text messaging, offering various flavors for different use cases including workplace applications. This matters to digital workplace folks because messaging is where employees actually live these days, so putting useful AI there beats forcing them into yet another app. The real question is whether these actually solve problems or just give us one more thing to manage in Slack while our email backlog screams for attention.

ai-at-work.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
ai-at-work.excerpt: An actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup — in a trend that's already popular in China. Experts question the long-term consequences if this becomes a trend in Hollywood, too.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: An actor just sold his digital likeness to a startup making short-form dramas, joining a practice that's already booming in China. This matters to digital workplace folks because deepfake technology and synthetic media are quietly becoming part of production workflows, raising real questions about consent, authentication, and how we verify who's actually in a meeting or on a call. Honestly, we're about to enter an era where your coworker might literally not be your coworker, and IT departments aren't ready for the security nightmare that creates.

ai-at-work.title: Sovereignty starts with data, not chips, says Stuttgart AI factory chief
ai-at-work.excerpt: A sovereign AI factory is only as valuable as the companies that can actually get onto it. Across Europe, publicly funded AI factories are racing to give startups and small manufacturers supercomputer
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Europe's building publicly funded AI factories to give smaller companies access to serious computing power without getting locked into one vendor or compromising their data. This matters because digital workplace leaders need to understand that infrastructure sovereignty isn't just about owning hardware, it's about maintaining control over how information flows through your organization. The irony here is thick: we finally built the computers, but the real competitive advantage went to whoever figured out the boring data governance part first.

digital-culture.title: 11 career decisions high performers regret making too late
digital-culture.excerpt: Some career decisions become costly only after too much time has passed. The following insights, from experts in the field, reveal which moves high performers often wish they had made sooner, from pro
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company rounded up career regrets from high performers, basically confirming that waiting too long to delegate, protect your health, build networks, and ask for help costs you dearly down the road. This matters to digital workplace folks because we're the ones building the systems and cultures that either enable or prevent people from making these moves early. Here's the thing: most of these regrets are preventable with decent workplace design and a manager who isn't terrified of losing control, so stop waiting for permission.

digital-culture.title: The one workplace time-suck even artificial intelligence can’t fix
digital-culture.excerpt: AI can instantaneously crunch numbers, analyze information, and write emails. One thing it still can’t do? Save you the time spent in meetings. Gallup surveyed 21,648 U.S. employees and found that amo
digital-culture.dwp_take: AI is saving knowledge workers time on data work and writing, but meetings remain untouched by automation. This matters because if we're serious about reclaiming worker time and productivity, we need to stop pretending technology alone will fix our meeting addiction. Here's the truth: we don't have a meeting problem, we have a decision-making problem, and no chatbot can fix what's really a cultural failure to run tight, purposeful gatherings.
